title: Air travel and the offsets people buy

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: The airline added a four-pound offset box at checkout and I genuinely don't know whether ticking it does anything.

turns.speaker: Nils
turns.text: Four pounds for a long-haul flight tells you most of what you need to know.

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: The audits have been brutal. One review of forest offset projects found the large majority hadn't prevented anything, because the trees weren't going to be cut down anyway.

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: So you're paying to protect a forest that was already safe.

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: And it counts on a balance sheet as a tonne removed, which is worse than doing nothing, because doing nothing doesn't come with a claim attached.

turns.speaker: Nils
turns.text: Removal offsets are different, in fairness. Actual carbon taken out and stored, priced properly, are somewhere over a hundred pounds a tonne.

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: Which would make my four-pound box about forty pounds.

turns.speaker: Nils
turns.text: Roughly, and nobody would tick it, which is precisely why it's priced where it is.

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: The deeper problem is what it does to the person. There's decent evidence that buying an offset makes people fly more, not less.

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: Exactly that. You've paid, so it's handled.

turns.speaker: Nils
turns.text: I'd rather the money went into fuel research and the airline just told me the flight has a cost I can't undo.

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: That's a harder sentence to put next to a checkout button.

points: Airlines offer cheap carbon offsets at checkout, around four pounds for a long-haul flight.
Tom cites audits finding most forest offset projects prevented nothing, because the trees were not under threat.
Such offsets are worse than inaction because they carry a false claim of a tonne removed.
Nils distinguishes genuine removal offsets, which cost over a hundred pounds a tonne, meaning an honest price would be roughly ten times what is charged.
Tom raises moral licensing: evidence suggests buying offsets increases rather than reduces flying.
Nils would prefer the money funded fuel research alongside an honest statement that the flight's cost cannot be undone.
